user_prompt:
Brand: Canva
Client topic: the first paycheck

Four candidate campaign directions were written for this brief. Candidate C2 was chosen and then developed into the final proposal below.

Candidates:
C1. Welcome to Payday: Flip the lens to employers. The first paycheck is the moment a new hire decides whether they belong, yet it usually arrives with silence or a PDF. Canva launches a 'First Payday Kit' for managers and small business owners: a personal note, a visual 'what this means' explainer, a team shout-out and a celebratory moment, all customisable in minutes. The message: 'Make the first paycheck feel like a first.'

C2. The Paycheck, Explained: Pay stubs are among the most important and least designed documents of adult life. Canva publicly redesigns the first-paycheck experience: a 'Pay Stub Makeover' that turns the gross-to-net shock into a clear, friendly visual story, plus free templates employers and first-timers can use to explain a paycheck in plain, visual language. The platform is 'Design is how things make sense.'

C3. First Paid Pixel: Celebrate the first time someone is paid for something they made. Canva invites people to share the first design that earned them money (a lawn-care flyer, a bake-sale menu, a band poster) next to the first paycheck it produced, and builds a living archive of 'first paid work' that proves creativity can be a livelihood.

C4. Official: The first paycheck is the moment imposter feelings meet proof: you now officially have a job. Canva makes 'Official' a ritual, a first-job identity kit generated the week the first paycheck lands: a business card, a LinkedIn banner, a name badge, a 'first day to first paycheck' recap video. The idea is that you stop pretending once you can show it.

Final proposal:
Title: The Paycheck, Explained
Your first paycheck is a small miracle, and a total mystery. You worked hard, and then a dense document shows a much smaller number than you expected. Canva redesigns that moment. We publicly give the pay stub a makeover, turning the gross-to-net shock into a clear, friendly visual story, and release free templates that employers, HR teams and small business owners can use to explain pay in plain, visual language, with a welcome note and team shout-out built in. It runs as makeover reveals, creator explainers, employer toolkits and OOH that mimics ugly pay stubs. Everything uses fictional data and explains rather than advises. The platform: design is how things make sense.

user_prompt:
Brand: Mastercard
Client topic: loneliness

Four candidate campaign directions were written for this brief. Candidate C2 was chosen and then developed into the final proposal below.

Candidates:
C1. The Lonely Hours: Use aggregate, anonymised Mastercard insights to map when and where cities feel emptiest, such as Sunday 3pm or the first Friday after a move, and publish a 'loneliness map' that councils, venues and brands use to open doors at those hours. The campaign is built around the discovery and the civic response.

C2. Pay Together: A small gift of money that can only be spent when two people are physically together. One person sends a 'Together' gift (a coffee, a haircut, a bowl of noodles) via a virtual Mastercard in an app, and it only activates when both phones are present at the same local independent venue. The payment itself becomes the invitation, so no one has to awkwardly ask someone to meet. An 'Open Tap' version pairs people with community partners such as befriending charities, neighbourhood groups or new-parent circles for those who have no one to send it to.

C3. The Second Seat: Every Priceless experience, dining offer or event perk Mastercard already gives cardholders is redesigned to include a 'second seat', and cardholders are nudged to give that seat to someone outside their usual circle, such as a neighbour, a colleague who has just moved or an older person from a partner charity.

C4. Regulars: Recognise that the corner cafe, barber and market stall are some of the last places where people are known by name. Launch a 'Regulars' programme in which Mastercard funds small independents to formalise being a regular: a reserved 'regulars' counter or table, names on a wall, and staff training for gentle check-ins. Cardholders can mark places as their 'regular'.

Final proposal:
Title: Pay Together
Money that only works when you're together. One person sends a small virtual Mastercard gift (a coffee, a haircut, a bowl of noodles) that only unlocks when both people confirm they're at the same local independent venue. The gift is the invitation, so nobody has to awkwardly ask. For people with no one to send it to, Open Tap lets befriending charities and community groups hold gift pools and arrange safe, public meetings with volunteers or neighbours. Venues get a simple Together table and a welcome guide, and an opt-in 'Next Time' gift encourages a second meeting. Piloted in one city, it is judged on meetings made and repeated, not on spend. It turns Priceless from a slogan into a payment that is worthless alone.

Brand: Mastercard
Client topic: loneliness

Four candidate campaign directions were written for this brief. Candidate C2 was chosen and then developed into the final proposal below.

Candidates:
C1. Priceless Regulars: Loneliness eases when you are known somewhere. Mastercard backs the 'third places' (barbers, cafes, diners) where staff recognise you, by helping small merchants host low-pressure regular hours and by celebrating the people who have been regulars for years. Regular status becomes a form of belonging.

C2. The Covered Invite: Make reaching out free and easy to accept. Any cardholder can send a digital invitation to a coffee, a meal or a class, and Mastercard covers the guest's first item at participating local merchants. The invite says, in effect, 'It's covered. Just come.' It removes the two main reasons people don't send or accept invitations: cost and the feeling of being a burden.

C3. The Quiet Index: Use aggregated, anonymised Mastercard Economics Institute data to publish a city-by-city picture of solo versus shared spending, and use it to show where social life is thinning out. The findings are given to city governments and community groups as a tool for investing in places and events that bring people together.

C4. Someone Real: Romance and friendship scams prey on loneliness. Mastercard works with issuers so that when payment patterns suggest someone is being groomed, they get a call or message from a trained human who talks with them rather than just blocking the card. The campaign tells the story that protecting people from scammers also means noticing when they are lonely.

Final proposal:
Title: It's Covered
People don't just stop going out; they stop asking. Cost and the fear of being a burden quietly kill invitations on both sides. 'It's Covered' lets any Mastercard cardholder send a digital invitation to a coffee, meal or class at a local merchant, and Mastercard pays for the guest's first item. The message is simple: it's covered, just come. Guests need no Mastercard card, and each guest gets one invite to pass on, so receiving becomes giving. Merchants fill quiet hours and offer a warm welcome; community groups and charities can send invites on behalf of people without someone to ask. Themed invites (new neighbour, old friend, first one back) and holiday peaks keep it fresh. Capped, fraud-protected and piloted in a few markets, with stories centred on the people at the table, never on the offer.

user_prompt:
Brand: Dior
Client topic: repair and reuse

Four candidate campaign directions were written for this brief. Candidate C4 was chosen and then developed into the final proposal below.

Candidates:
C1. The Open Atelier: For a limited run in several cities, Dior's craftspeople repair anyone's beloved garment, from any brand or none, in a pop-up atelier. The only price of entry is the story of why the item matters. The campaign shows the House giving its rarest skill to ordinary clothing.

C2. Lineage: Every Dior piece is given a living passport that records its owners, repairs and occasions. When an owner is done with it, the House restores it and certifies it for its next custodian, positioning the piece as something held in trust rather than owned outright. The campaign celebrates the chain of owners, such as the 'third owner of this Saddle bag'.

C3. Mended by Dior: A signature visible mend, a Dior-designed stitch or embroidered motif (star, muguet, bee), turns the repair itself into a collectible mark. Instead of hiding the damage, the House repairs it with a designed flourish, so a mended piece reads as more distinctive than a pristine one.

C4. Second Fitting: Dior built its name on the first fitting, the moment a piece is made for you. Second Fitting offers the next one. Any Dior piece, bought new, inherited or found secondhand, can return to the atelier to be re-fitted for the life its owner is living now: a Bar jacket let out for a new body, a mother's coat recut for a daughter, a worn Lady Dior re-edged. Each finished piece gets a dated, signed 'Second Fitting' label. The campaign is told through real transformations and the named hands that perform them.

Final proposal:
Title: Second Fitting
Dior made its name on the first fitting, the moment a piece is made for you. Second Fitting offers the next one. Any genuine Dior piece, bought new, inherited or found secondhand, can return to the atelier to be refitted for the life its owner lives now: a Bar jacket let out for a new body, a mother's coat recut for her daughter, a worn Lady Dior re-edged. Each finished piece receives a dated, signed Second Fitting label. The campaign tells real transformations through the named hands of the petites mains, across film, boutique, client ledger and press. Repair becomes a couture ritual, and keeping a Dior piece becomes the status act.

A: artisan-signed / visible repair mark as status signal
B: repair history record, passport, certified resale
C: public repair of anyone's clothes, repair teaching, open atelier, store closure day
D: new collection / runway from archive, offcuts or clients' clothes

F: Second Fitting: couture fitting ritual extended over the garment's life / to next owner

user_prompt:
Brand: Dior
Client topic: repair and reuse

Four candidate campaign directions were written for this brief. Candidate C2 was chosen and then developed into the final proposal below.

Candidates:
C1. The Flaw Collection: A provocative couture show built on damage: moth holes, torn hems, worn elbows and faded creases from real clients' beloved pieces. Designers reinterpret each flaw as a deliberate couture signature, and the original owners attend the show to see their pieces reborn.

C2. The Extra Inch: Inside well-made couture garments, hidden seam allowances give the piece room to be taken in, let out and re-fitted over decades. The campaign reveals this concealed inch as Dior's quiet promise of a long life. It treats the garment as something designed to change with its owner, and it frames repair, refitting and re-gifting as the 'next inch' of the story.

C3. Second Fitting: A house-certified pre-owned programme in which returned Dior pieces are authenticated, restored and re-fitted by the atelier for a new owner. Each piece carries a numbered label recording its previous wearers. Provenance becomes the new status symbol, and being 'owner number two' is positioned as a mark of taste.

C4. Hands That Remember: Put the repairers, not the designers, in the spotlight. Each repair is credited by first name and shown in intimate close-up. The campaign celebrates the atelier people who restore, re-hem, re-line and revive, positioning repair as the highest form of couture skill.

Final proposal:
Title: The Extra Inch

user_prompt:
Brand: Canva
Client topic: the first paycheck

Four candidate campaign directions were written for this brief. Candidate C3 was chosen and then developed into the final proposal below.

Candidates:
C1. Pay It Forward Deck: Invite people to make something for the next first jobber with their own first paycheck story: a one-page guide, a welcome poster, a 'what I wish I knew' card for new hires. Experienced workers design advice for newcomers, and Canva connects them to schools, youth programmes and employers. The paycheck becomes the start of a chain of mentorship, not just a reward.

C2. Proof You Belong: Name the real first-paycheck tension: you got paid, but do you feel like you belong? Show that new hires earn their place through small visible work, like the deck nobody else wanted to make. Canva becomes the tool for that 'proof of belonging', and the campaign celebrates the unglamorous first deliverable as the true initiation. The reveal: your first paycheck is the company's way of saying 'we believe you', and the first thing you make is you saying 'I believe it too'.

C3. The First Thing You Made: Reframe the first paycheck as payment for the first thing you made at work. Invite people to revisit their first work creation (a flyer for the shop, a menu, a slide for the boss, a rota) and the paycheck it helped earn. People share the artefact next to the pay moment, and Canva lets them recreate or remix it as a 'first paycheck' keepsake. The idea: every career starts with something you made.

C4. The Payslip Redesign: The payslip is the most important document most people receive, and one of the worst designed: confusing, cold, full of codes. Canva redesigns the first payslip into something a person actually understands and wants to keep, with plain language, clear visuals and a keepsake version. It is a bold provocation: if design can make a first paycheck feel like an achievement, why are the documents of work so bad? Employers can adopt Canva-designed payslip and offer-letter templates.

Final proposal:
Title: Paid for Making
Your first paycheck wasn't a reward for showing up. It was payment for the first thing you made. A shop flyer that earned £38. A hand-drawn rota. A menu board. A slide the boss needed by Friday. 'Paid for Making' invites people to put that first creation beside the pay it earned, rebuilding it from memory if it's lost, and remix it in Canva into a keepsake: the thing, the amount, the story. Creators and well-known figures seed the specific stories first, so the campaign leads with people, not templates. First jobbers capture theirs as it happens, while managers and parents revisit their own. Employers join by turning a new hire's first-week deliverable into a welcome ritual, celebrated and shared with the team. Every career starts with something you made.

C4. Tap Together: A prepaid 'On Me' experience that only works when two people are present. Tapping together becomes a gesture of reconnection with a friend, a neighbour, a former colleague or a relative.

Title: Tap Together
Loneliness rarely asks for company, so Tap Together makes offering it easy. Anyone can send a friend, neighbour, former colleague or relative an 'On Me' invitation to a coffee, haircut, cinema ticket or bowl of noodles at a local business. The treat unlocks only when both people tap their cards or phones at the same terminal during the same visit, so it can't be enjoyed alone. The sender takes the social risk, and the receiver can say yes without admitting anything. The money starts it, but the value is the time shared. A commitment device makes reaching out and following through easier.

C2. The Second Seat: Restaurants and cafés keep a 'second seat' at a communal table for solo diners. A Mastercard cardholder can pre-pay for a seat or a meal that a stranger can claim, an adaptation of the 'suspended coffee' tradition, so that eating alone becomes an invitation instead of a stigma.

C3. The Slow Lane: A brand confession turned into a movement: 'We made paying faster. Not everything should be.' Partner grocers, pharmacies and markets designate one checkout lane as unhurried, with a sign reading 'This lane takes its time'. Cashiers opt in and are given the time to chat, and the terminal has an optional 'Slow Tap' mode that swaps the efficient beep for a warmer, human pause. Anyone can use the lane, whether they want conversation, are not in a rush, or just like it.

C4. Regulars: Celebrate the oldest cure for loneliness: being a regular. Mastercard creates a 'Regulars' mark for local cafés, barbers, bakeries and shops that commit to knowing their customers' names and orders. Using aggregate, anonymised insight, it shows how many people have a place where they are known and rallies cities to protect those places.

Final proposal:
Title: The Slow Lane
Mastercard made paying faster. Now it admits that not everything should be. In partner grocers and pharmacies, one checkout lane is marked 'This lane takes its time'. Cashiers opt in, get time and recognition as Slow Lane hosts, and are free to chat. Anyone can use it, so nobody has to say they're lonely. A 'Slow Tap' mode swaps the efficient beep for a warmer pause, using Mastercard's own terminal and sound. It starts as a measured pilot with a loneliness charity, runs at flexible hours, and publishes its results. It can grow into Slow Hour, Slow Day and a sonic signature. Candidates:

Mastercard enables 'Priceless Plans', small refundable deposits that friends or groups put down for a dinner, class or trip, and the deposit is returned when everyone shows up. C2. The Second Seat: Restaurants and cafés keep a 'second seat' at a communal table for solo diners. A Mastercard cardholder can pre-pay for a seat or a meal that a stranger can claim, an adaptation of the 'suspended coffee' tradition, so that eating alone becomes an invitation instead of a stigma.

C3. The Slow Lane: A brand confession turned into a movement: 'We made paying faster. Not everything should be.' Partner grocers, pharmacies and markets designate one checkout lane as unhurried, with a sign reading 'This lane takes its time'. Cashiers opt in and are given the time to chat, and the terminal has an optional 'Slow Tap' mode that swaps the efficient beep for a warmer, human pause. Anyone can use the lane, whether they want conversation, are not in a rush, or just like it.

C4. Regulars: Celebrate the oldest cure for loneliness: being a regular. Mastercard creates a 'Regulars' mark for local cafés, barbers, bakeries and shops that commit to knowing their customers' names and orders. Using aggregate, anonymised insight, it shows how many people have a place where they are known and rallies cities to protect those places.

Final proposal:
Title: The Slow Lane
For many people, the checkout is the only conversation of the day. Mastercard made paying faster. Now it says: not everything should be. An optional Slow Tap setting swaps the quick beep for a softer, longer tone, so paying feels like a pause. Anyone can use the lane, so nobody has to say they are lonely. C1. Take Your Time (the unhurried acceptance mark): For many people, the only human conversation of the day happens at a till. Mastercard creates a second acceptance mark for places that choose to be unhurried: cafés, barbers, corner shops and market stalls where staff are happy to chat. The sonic logo gets a longer, slower 'lingering' version for these places, and 'Take your time' becomes a recognisable signal.

C2. Open Seat: Make doing things alone feel designed-for, not like a penalty. Partner restaurants, cinemas and event venues hold one open seat at shared tables or in rows, bookable through Priceless Experiences. Cardholders can book 'for one' and be seated in a way that makes the meal or show a social possibility, not an awkward absence.

C3. Third Place Fund: Use Mastercard's aggregated, anonymised economic insight to map where neighbourhoods are losing their social infrastructure, such as cafés, laundrettes and community shops. Fund and promote the 'third places' that act as informal community hubs. Publish a high street connection index and back local places with grants and visibility.

C4. Tap Together: A prepaid 'On Me' experience that only works when two people are present. Anyone can send an invitation to a coffee, a walk-in cinema ticket, a haircut or a bowl of noodles at a local business. It is redeemed only when the sender's and receiver's cards tap at the same terminal within the same visit. The generosity cannot be consumed alone. Tapping together becomes a gesture of reconnection with a friend, a neighbour, a former colleague or a relative.

Final proposal:
Title: Tap Together
Many people are lonely but won't ask for company. Tap Together flips that: instead of asking, you offer. Send a friend, neighbour, ex-colleague or relative an 'On Me' invitation to a coffee, a haircut, a cinema seat or a bowl of noodles at a local business. It can only be redeemed when both your cards tap at the same terminal during the same visit. The treat can't be enjoyed alone. The sender takes the social risk, and the receiver can say yes without admitting anything. Mastercard's most familiar gesture, the tap, becomes a sign of togetherness. Participating shops get footfall, a slow 'lingering' sonic logo marks each shared tap, and shared visits become the campaign's measure of success. Pilot in a few neighbourhoods, then scale through festive gifting, charity partners and creators.

user_prompt:

Client topic: the first paycheck

Four candidate campaign directions were written for this brief. Candidate C3 was chosen and then developed into the final proposal below.

Candidates:
C1. Pay It Forward Deck: Invite people to make something for the next first jobber with their own first paycheck story: a one-page guide, a welcome poster, a 'what I wish I knew' card for new hires. Experienced workers design advice for newcomers, and Canva connects them to schools, youth programmes and employers. The paycheck becomes the start of a chain of mentorship, not just a reward.

C2. Proof You Belong: Name the real first-paycheck tension: you got paid, but do you feel like you belong? Show that new hires earn their place through small visible work, like the deck nobody else wanted to make. Canva becomes the tool for that 'proof of belonging', and the campaign celebrates the unglamorous first deliverable as the true initiation. The reveal: your first paycheck is the company's way of saying 'we believe you', and the first thing you make is you saying 'I believe it too'.

C3. The First Thing You Made: Reframe the first paycheck as payment for the first thing you made at work. Invite people to revisit their first work creation (a flyer for the shop, a menu, a slide for the boss, a rota) and the paycheck it helped earn. People share the artefact next to the pay moment, and Canva lets them recreate or remix it as a 'first paycheck' keepsake. The idea: every career starts with something you made.

C4. The Payslip Redesign: The payslip is the most important document most people receive, and one of the worst designed: confusing, cold, full of codes. Canva redesigns the first payslip into something a person actually understands and wants to keep, with plain language, clear visuals and a keepsake version. It is a bold provocation: if design can make a first paycheck feel like an achievement, why are the documents of work so bad? Employers can adopt Canva-designed payslip and offer-letter templates.

Final proposal:
Title: Paid to Make
Your first paycheck wasn't payment for showing up. It was payment for the first thing you made: the chalkboard menu, the shop flyer, the rota, the slide the boss needed by Friday. Canva invites everyone to pair that first creation with the pay it earned. Can't find it? Rebuild it from memory in Canva, or share a handwritten price list or sign. The result is a 'First Make' keepsake: the artefact, the story, the date and, if you choose, the amount. The campaign launches with sharp real stories from recognisable names and ordinary workers, not templates. Employers join through onboarding: new hires design their first deliverable or welcome ritual and mark their first payday with a keepsake. Managers and parents share theirs too, so every generation says the same thing: every career starts with something you made.

Title: Owe Me One
When you split a bill or cover a friend's coffee, a new option appears beside 'Send': Settle in person. Instead of moving money, the app sets a shared date, and a Mastercard chime confirms it. A payments brand choosing not to complete the transaction is the provocation: time with people is the one currency that can't be sent digitally. Partner cafes hold the table and add a small perk. If the meetup slips, a gentle nudge offers to reschedule or pay as usual, so nobody is left out of pocket. Phase one is a one-city pilot with a P2P partner and a public counter of meetups kept. 'Who do you owe one?' carries the idea into social and content, inviting everyone to see a friend they've been meaning to.

Codebook of core mechanisms for this brief (what the idea does to address the topic):
A1: recognition at the tap: terminal shows chosen name / regular signal
A2: Regulars programme: certify / fund local merchants that know their regulars
A3: Slow Lane / Take Your Time: unhurried checkout, slower payment sound
B: paid invitation: pre-paid treat or plan, often unlocks only when both tap together
C: settle in person: a debt / IOU becomes a reason to meet
D: open seat / communal table for solo diners or strangers
E: connection index / loneliness map from aggregated spend data
F: missed you: merchant or contact nudged when a routine lapses
G: solo tax: remove the extra price of being alone
H: commitment money: shared pots, deposits, caps, social budgets, rewards for togetherness
Z: other (single occurrences)
